intuition:
# Four-qubit error-detecting code

## Essence

The code asks only two questions of four physical qubits:

`S_X = XXXX`, and `S_Z = ZZZZ`.

Their overlap contains four qubits, so the four local anticommutation signs
cancel and the two operators commute. The simultaneous `+1` eigenspace has
dimension four: it carries two logical qubits. A convenient exported logical
basis is

`Xbar_1=XX__`, `Zbar_1=_Z_Z`, `Xbar_2=X_X_`, `Zbar_2=__ZZ`.

Each operator commutes with both stabilizers; within each numbered pair the
supports meet once and therefore anticommute, while the cross-pairs meet an
even number of times. The constructor exports these supports, and the
reproduction script at `atlas/four_two_two/pedagogy/reproduce.py` checks the
complete symplectic table.

The key idea is not merely that the distance is two. It is what information
the syndrome retains. A single `X_i` fault flips only `S_Z`, independent of
`i`; a single `Z_i` fault flips only `S_X`; and a single `Y_i` fault flips
both. The syndrome identifies the Pauli type but forgets the position. Thus
the code detects every single-qubit Pauli fault, yet cannot repair an
unknown-position fault from these two bits alone. If the position arrives as
side information—an erasure flag—the same block can correct the fault
([Grassl, Beth, and Pellizzari](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9610042)).

**One sentence.** The `[[4,2,2]]` code spends two global parities to preserve
two logical qubits, obtaining universal single-site detection but no
single-site address.

## Design problem

Suppose four carriers should hold more than one logical qubit while exposing
any fault confined to one carrier. Full unknown-location correction is too
ambitious at this length and rate: correction must distinguish alternatives,
whereas detection needs only separate the no-error subspace from the union of
error spaces.

The two global checks solve exactly the weaker problem. Every nonidentity
single-qubit Pauli anticommutes with at least one stabilizer. Therefore its
action takes the codespace into an orthogonal syndrome sector. But there are
twelve such Pauli faults and only three nonzero two-bit syndromes. The
compression is deliberate: the block reports “an X-like, Z-like, or Y-like
component occurred,” not “qubit `i` failed.”

This distinction is operational. A postselected experiment discards every
nonzero-syndrome run and never needs a correction location. A known-erasure
protocol receives that location from loss, leakage conversion, or another
flag. A syndrome-only correction rule must guess; for example, correcting an
actual `X_j` as though it were `X_i` leaves `X_i X_j`, a zero-syndrome
weight-two logical operator when `i != j`. The full error-set comparison is
worked in [detection versus correction](pedagogy/detection-versus-correction.md).

## Derivation chain

1. Write one all-ones row in each CSS sector: `H_X=H_Z=[1 1 1 1]`.
   Their binary inner product is zero, so the CSS checks commute.
2. The two check rows are independent in the symplectic stabilizer matrix.
   Four physical qubits minus rank two leaves two encoded qubits.
3. Every weight-one Pauli has a nonzero syndrome. The explicit syndrome table
   contains three values, each repeated at all four positions.
4. Each exported logical has weight two, commutes with the stabilizers, and
   lies outside their row space. This supplies a weight-two normalizer witness.
   Since no weight-one Pauli is in the normalizer, the exact distance is two.
5. The logical computational basis can be chosen as

   `|00bar>=(|0000>+|1111>)/sqrt(2)`,

   `|01bar>=(|1010>+|0101>)/sqrt(2)`,

   `|10bar>=(|1100>+|0011>)/sqrt(2)`,

   `|11bar>=(|0110>+|1001>)/sqrt(2)`.

   Each pair is exchanged by `XXXX`, has even parity under `ZZZZ`, and has
   the eigenvalues declared by `Zbar_1,Zbar_2`. Published papers sometimes
   choose different weight-two representatives; multiplying by a stabilizer
   or applying a logical symplectic relabeling changes the presentation, not
   the code.
6. Rains proves that the optimal length-four, distance-two quantum code is
   unique up to local equivalence and places it in the even-length
   `[[2m,2m-2,2]]` global-parity family
   ([Rains](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9704043)). The Atlas identity is the
   exact binary CSS stabilizer block above, not every locally equivalent
   presentation and not every member of that family.

The algebra, syndrome enumeration, codeword eigenvalues, exact distance, and
logical Clifford conjugations are rerun in
[the Level-2 derivation map](pedagogy/derivations.md).

## Multiple pictures

**Global parity.** `XXXX` asks whether the phase-flip component has odd
parity; `ZZZZ` asks the same of the bit-flip component. This is the shortest
route to the syndrome table.

**Binary CSS matrix.** The two one-row all-ones matrices make rank and
commutation transparent. They also reveal that the square in the viewer is
only an incidence arrangement: every check touches every qubit, so no
two-dimensional locality follows from the drawing.

**Four Bell-like branches.** The computational codewords are complements
paired by `XXXX`. The two logical bits select which complementary pair is
occupied. This picture is useful for preparation and readout, but a protocol
must still specify which logical degree of freedom is data and whether the
other is protected, fixed, or treated as gauge.

**Syndrome quotient.** The twelve weight-one Pauli labels collapse to three
nonzero syndrome classes. Detection succeeds because none collapse onto the
zero class. Correction fails because several distinct errors collapse onto
one another and their pairwise products can act logically.

**Erasure channel.** Once a classical flag supplies the faulty position, the
relevant error set contains only `I,X_i,Y_i,Z_i` for one fixed `i`. Their
pairwise products remain supported at that known position and are detected by
the distance-two code, so the Knill–Laflamme conditions can be satisfied. The
side-information bit is part of the channel contract, not an implementation
detail.

**Iceberg specialization.** The same global X and Z parities define the
`[[k+2,k,2]]` Iceberg family. This block is its smallest nontrivial member.
That relation does not license importing family-scale Hamiltonian,
connectivity, or experiment claims into this fixed block; those belong to the
corresponding protocol and size.

## Why these parameters

**Length and dimension.** The constructor has four Pauli columns and two
independent stabilizer rows. Direct GF(2) rank gives `k=4-2=2`. The verifier
recomputes both values from the exported `CheckMatrix`; neither is accepted
from prose.

**Distance.** Every weight-one `X`, `Y`, or `Z` anticommutes with a global
check, giving the lower bound `d>=2`. The exported `XX__` commutes with both
checks, is not a stabilizer, and acts as `Xbar_1`, giving `d<=2`. Together the
bounds prove `d=2`; exhaustive distance enumeration independently agrees.

**Why two syndrome bits are enough for detection.** Detection asks only
whether the syndrome is zero. The two-bit alphabet has a zero value and three
nonzero values, exactly enough to separate the three nonidentity Pauli types
when position is discarded.

**Why they are not enough for correction.** Unknown-location correction
would need the error subspaces for alternatives such as `X_i` and `X_j` to be
distinguishable or logically equivalent. They have the same syndrome, and
`X_i X_j` is generally a nontrivial normalizer element. The collision is
therefore logical, not just a limitation of a particular lookup-table
implementation.

## Failure modes

- **Treating a detector as a corrector.** Mapping a nonzero syndrome to an
  arbitrary position silently inserts a logical fault whenever the guess is
  wrong. The valid syndrome-only action is reject, flag, or request more
  information.
- **Forgetting measurement faults.** The static distance statement assumes
  trustworthy parity outcomes. A circuit-level protocol needs ancillas,
  ordering, repeated or verified measurements, and a decoder for that richer
  record. None is implied by the bare matrix.
- **Protecting only one logical qubit without saying so.** Several early
  demonstrations fix or gauge the second encoded degree of freedom so that a
  fault-tolerant circuit protects one chosen logical qubit. Their result is
  real but narrower than arbitrary operations on both logical qubits
  ([Linke et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.06946)).
- **Borrowing a concatenated threshold.** The
  `[[4,2,2]]`-concatenated Toric code is a different construction with a
  growing outer family, extraction circuit, and decoder. Its threshold is not
  a property of this isolated block
  ([Criger and Terhal](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.04062)).
- **Equating a face with a code family.** A four-body check may occur inside a
  Surface or color-code layout. Shared local support does not identify the
  whole code, its boundaries, its logical space, or a typed Atlas relation.
- **Calling the square a lattice.** The check support is global. The viewer's
  square makes four logical edges legible; it does not assert nearest-neighbor
  stabilizer measurement.

## Operations story

Uniform Clifford layers have unusually dense logical action because both
logical qubits occupy one small block. Under `H` on every physical qubit,
`Xbar_1` maps to `Zbar_2`, `Xbar_2` maps to `Zbar_1`, and conversely. The
logical action is `H` on both logical qubits followed by their swap. Under
uniform physical `S`, the X logicals acquire the opposite Z logical while Z
logicals stay fixed, which is logical `CZ` up to tracked phases.

Between two aligned blocks, pairwise physical CNOT preserves the joint
stabilizer group and implements CNOT on each corresponding logical pair. This
is an algebraic transversal statement. Routing, preparation, syndrome
extraction, and correlated faults remain protocol costs.

The block also supports a ten-input/two-output Hadamard-eigenstate
magic-state distillation routine
([Meier, Eastin, and Knill](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4221)). That ratio and
its error suppression belong to the complete accepted-round protocol, not to
the code parameters alone. Later superconducting work prepared an encoded CZ
resource here and then moved it through a code transition; the reported
beyond-break-even result belongs to the combined preparation, detection,
deformation, and teleportation stack
([Gupta et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13581)).

See [operations and realizations](pedagogy/operations-and-realizations.md) for
the conjugation table and evidence boundaries.

## Litmus questions

**Q1:** What does the syndrome of a single-qubit error reveal?
**A:** Its Pauli component—X-like, Z-like, or both—but not its physical
position.

**Q2:** Why does nonzero syndrome prove detection but not correction?
**A:** Detection only separates the error space from the codespace. Correction
must also distinguish or harmlessly identify different errors within the same
syndrome, and same-type faults at different positions can differ logically.

**Q3:** How can a distance-two code correct one erasure?
**A:** The erasure channel supplies the position. For that restricted error
set, all pairwise products are supported on one known site and are detected.

**Q4:** Give both halves of the distance proof.
**A:** Every weight-one Pauli has nonzero syndrome, while `XX__` is a
weight-two normalizer element outside the stabilizer.

**Q5:** Does the trapped-ion demonstration protect two arbitrary logical
qubits fault tolerantly?
**A:** No. Its protocol protects one chosen logical qubit and treats the other
encoded degree of freedom as gauge.

**Q6:** Is this entry the distance-two rotated Surface code?
**A:** No. The familiar four-data rotated patch encodes one logical qubit and
has boundary checks. This entry has only two global checks and encodes two.

**Q7:** Is a Toric-code threshold cited for a `[[4,2,2]]`-concatenated
construction a threshold of this block?
**A:** No. The outer family, circuit noise model, and decoder create the
asymptotic threshold statement.

**Q8:** What does uniform physical `S` do logically?
**A:** It preserves both logical Z operators and attaches each to the other
logical qubit's Z under X conjugation, which is logical `CZ` up to phases.

# Four-qubit code — Level-2 map

Each page below answers one question completely and keeps executable algebra
separate from literature claims.

1. [How the stabilizers, logical basis, codewords, and distance fit together](stabilizer-and-logical-basis.md).
2. [Why single-site detection does not imply unknown-site correction](detection-versus-correction.md).
3. [Which Clifford actions are intrinsic and which experimental claims are protocol-scoped](operations-and-realizations.md).
4. [Which neighboring descriptions are presentations, family extensions, or different codes](representations-and-boundaries.md).

## Reproduction contract

Run from the repository root:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
python atlas/four_two_two/pedagogy/reproduce.py
make verify-entry E=atlas/four_two_two
```

The script imports the shipped constructor. It recomputes CSS ranks and exact
distance, enumerates all single-qubit syndromes, verifies the logical
symplectic table and codeword eigenvalues, checks the erasure
Knill–Laflamme matrices, conjugates the logical basis under physical `H`, `S`,
and inter-block CNOT, and validates both Scene v2 frames. It exits nonzero at
the first disagreement.

The provenance split is deliberate:

- `n`, `k`, `d`, CSS commutation, syndromes, logical representatives, and
  Clifford conjugations are machine-verified.
- The one-erasure interpretation is theorem-backed and then checked on the
  exported finite code.
- Distillation performance and hardware outcomes remain claimed by their
  primary sources. They are not inferred from the static check matrix.

# Detection, correction, and erasure side information

## One theorem

The exported `[[4,2,2]]` block detects the complete set of single-qubit Pauli
faults, cannot correct that set when the position is unknown, and can correct
an arbitrary error on one position when that position is supplied as erasure
side information.

These are three statements about three different error sets.

## The complete syndrome table

Order the syndrome bits as the anticommutation outcomes against
`(XXXX, ZZZZ)`. For every physical position `i`,

| error | syndrome |
|---|---|
| `X_i` | `(0,1)` |
| `Z_i` | `(1,0)` |
| `Y_i` | `(1,1)` |

All twelve nonidentity weight-one errors have nonzero syndrome, so all are
detected. The table has only three distinct nonzero rows: moving the error
does not change the result.

## Why a correction guess fails

For a correctable set `{E_a}`, the Knill–Laflamme condition requires

`P E_a^dagger E_b P = c_ab P`,

where `P` projects onto the codespace. Consider two same-type alternatives at
different unknown positions, `E_a=X_i` and `E_b=X_j`. Their product is
`X_i X_j`. It commutes with the stabilizers and, for suitable `i,j`, is one
of the exported logical operators or differs from one by a stabilizer. Its
restriction to the codespace is not a scalar. Therefore the complete
unknown-position single-fault set violates the condition.

The syndrome collision and the theorem say the same thing in two languages.
If a lookup table guesses `i` but the error was at `j`, recovery leaves
`X_i X_j`. A nonzero detector outcome tells us to reject; it does not license
an arbitrary correction.

This is why the trapped-ion experiment uses postselection and explicitly
states that the code cannot locate an unknown error
([Linke et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.06946)).

## Why known erasure is different

Now suppose a classical record says position `i` was erased. The error set is
only `{I,X_i,Y_i,Z_i}`. Every product `E_a^dagger E_b` is either identity or
a Pauli supported at that same position. The nonidentity products have
nonzero syndrome, so their projection into the codespace vanishes; identity
projects to `P`. The Knill–Laflamme condition holds.

The recovery map must consume both pieces of information:

1. the known physical position, supplied by the channel or a conversion
   mechanism; and
2. the parity information needed to reconstruct the state.

Grassl, Beth, and Pellizzari define the erasure channel precisely as an
arbitrary error at a known position and give the four-qubit encoding
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9610042)). Gingrich and
collaborators use the two-to-four encoding in an optical loss-memory proposal
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0306098)). Neither source
turns the unknown-position Pauli detector into a one-error correcting code.

## Measurement faults are a fourth problem

The table above assumes perfect measurement of both global checks. A faulty
ancilla or entangling gate can corrupt the syndrome and propagate errors into
the data. A circuit-level detector therefore requires a preparation circuit,
gate ordering, ancilla verification or repeated checks, and a rule for the
resulting time history.

Gottesman frames small fault-tolerance experiments around precisely this
protocol-level criterion
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.03507)). The static block is an
ingredient. “Distance two” alone neither certifies nor refutes a particular
fault-tolerant preparation or postselected computation.

## Practical decision table

| available information | honest action |
|---|---|
| perfect syndrome, unknown position | accept zero; reject or flag nonzero |
| perfect syndrome plus known erasure position | location-aware recovery |
| noisy repeated outcomes | decode the specified circuit history |
| no syndrome measurement | no QEC claim from the encoding alone |

This table is the boundary carried into `card.yaml`: the two lookup rows name
different inputs and do not pretend to be one universal decoder.

documents.title: Logical operations and realization boundaries
documents.markdown:
# Logical operations and realization boundaries

## One theorem

For the exported logical basis, uniform physical `H` implements logical
`(H tensor H) SWAP`, uniform physical `S` implements logical `CZ` up to
Pauli phases, and pairwise physical CNOT between aligned blocks implements
parallel logical CNOT on the corresponding logical pairs.

These are exact Pauli-conjugation statements. Whether a laboratory circuit is
fault tolerant additionally depends on preparation, routing, extraction, and
postselection.

## Uniform physical H

Conjugation swaps X and Z on every physical qubit. Modulo the stabilizers,

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `Xbar_1=XX__` | `Zbar_2=__ZZ` |
| `Zbar_1=_Z_Z` | `Xbar_2=X_X_` |
| `Xbar_2=X_X_` | `Zbar_1=_Z_Z` |
| `Zbar_2=__ZZ` | `Xbar_1=XX__` |

For example, physical H sends `XX__` to `ZZ__`; multiplying by the stabilizer
`ZZZZ` gives `__ZZ`. Thus each logical qubit receives H and the two logical
labels are exchanged. Meier, Eastin, and Knill give the same logical action
in their chosen basis
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4221)).

## Uniform physical S

Ignoring the tracked Pauli phase, `S X S^dagger = XZ` and Z is fixed. Hence

`Xbar_1 -> Xbar_1 Zbar_2`, and

`Xbar_2 -> Zbar_1 Xbar_2`,

while both Z logicals stay fixed. This is exactly the Clifford conjugation
table of logical CZ. The reproduction script performs the binary symplectic
calculation modulo stabilizers rather than relying on these displayed
representatives.

## Inter-block physical CNOT

Under CNOT, control X acquires target X and target Z acquires control Z. Apply
the gate pairwise between two equally indexed blocks. Every X stabilizer on
the control acquires the corresponding target stabilizer, and every Z
stabilizer on the target acquires the corresponding control stabilizer, so
the joint stabilizer row space is preserved. The same rule acts on both
logical pairs and gives two parallel encoded CNOTs.

The statement is transversal in an interaction graph that provides aligned
pairs. It does not include motion, crosstalk, or correlated decoding.

## Magic-state protocols

Meier, Eastin, and Knill use this code in an accepted-round routine that
consumes ten noisy Hadamard eigenstates and outputs two improved states. The
transversal Clifford symmetries explain why the block is useful, but the
distillation claim also includes the preparation, measurements, acceptance
condition, and input-noise assumptions.

Gupta and collaborators prepare an encoded CZ resource in the four-qubit
block and then deform and teleport it into a one-logical-qubit code
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13581)). The code transition is a
protocol boundary: the reported beyond-break-even fidelity cannot be assigned
to bare `XXXX/ZZZZ` storage.

## What the experiments establish

- Linke and collaborators use four trapped-ion data qubits and an ancilla to
  demonstrate fault-tolerant preparation, measurement, and operation of one
  logical qubit. The other encoded degree of freedom is a gauge qubit, so the
  protocol does not claim arbitrary protected two-logical-qubit computation.
- Takita and collaborators demonstrate fault-tolerant preparation in a
  protected one-logical-qubit subspace on superconducting hardware. Again,
  the subsystem choice is part of the result.
- Vuillot and Roffe and collaborators show postselection benefits on IBM
  five-qubit devices using different circuit representations. Harper and
  Flammia benchmark logical Clifford gates and report an encoded-gate benefit,
  while also explaining that state preparation and measurement prevent an
  end-to-end below-threshold conclusion.

Primary records:
[Linke et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.06946),
[Takita et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.09259),
[Vuillot](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08957),
[Roffe et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.01866), and
[Harper–Flammia](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.02359).

## What the experiments do not establish

They do not give this fixed block an asymptotic threshold. A threshold needs a
growing family plus a specified noise model, syndrome circuit, decoder, and
observable. Criger and Terhal study such a tuple for a distinct
`[[4,2,2]]`-concatenated Toric construction
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.04062)); their threshold does not
transfer to this entry.

documents.title: Representations, variants, and identity boundaries
documents.markdown:
# Representations, variants, and identity boundaries

## Exact Atlas identity

This entry is the exact binary qubit CSS stabilizer code with generator row
space `span{XXXX, ZZZZ}`. Local Clifford changes, qubit permutations, logical
symplectic relabelings, circuit encoders, and different drawn squares may
present an equivalent code, but the constructor fixes one representative so
claims can be recomputed.

The four-term logical basis in the constructor is a presentation choice. The
stabilizer row space, logical dimension, and distance are identity-level
facts.

## Iceberg family

Rains describes the even-length optimal additive family with global X and Z
checks. Self, Benedetti, and Amaro call the resulting `[[k+2,k,2]]` family
Iceberg in an error-detected circuit setting
([Rains](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9704043),
[Self et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.06703)). At its smallest nontrivial
size it has exactly the two stabilizers exported here, so `special_case_of
iceberg` is a typed relation.

The direction matters: this entry is not widened to arbitrary `k`. A
family-scale penalty Hamiltonian or experiment must state whether its result
was actually obtained at the four-qubit member.

## Subsystem presentations

A protocol may designate one encoded qubit as protected data and the other as
gauge or a fixed spectator. Then the same four-qubit stabilizer space is used
as a `[[4,1,2]]` subsystem code for that protocol. Linke's trapped-ion
demonstration and Takita's superconducting preparation use this boundary
explicitly. The physical block is the same; the protected logical contract is
narrower.

This is not permission to rewrite the entry parameter as `k=1`. The
constructor still has a four-dimensional codespace. A protocol-level gauge
choice belongs in realizations and pedagogy.

## Coherent parity-check circuit

The CPC formalism gives an encoder/check circuit presentation of a
`[[4,2,2]]` detector. Roffe and collaborators implement such a presentation
on IBM hardware
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.01866)). CPC is a broader circuit
framework, not a second stabilizer identity and not a typed relation in the
current Atlas grammar.

## Neighboring codes that are not this entry

**Rotated Surface patch.** A four-data distance-two rotated patch commonly
encodes one logical qubit and contains boundary checks of smaller support. It
is not generated solely by the two global parities. A shared square drawing
does not establish a relation to the live `surface` entry.

**Color-code face.** One four-body face operator inside a 4.8.8 or triangular
color code is a local check, not the whole global-parity block. Removing
checks from a color-code layout can participate in a larger concatenated
construction, as in Criger–Terhal, but that construction is not a direct
relation from this block to `color_666` or `toric`.

**Five-qubit and Steane codes.** These are neighboring small stabilizer codes
with different lengths, dimensions, distances, and check row spaces. Being
listed together or used in comparative experiments is a bibliographic cousin
relation, not one of the typed algebraic Atlas relations.

**Error-prevention protocol.** Vaidman, Goldenberg, and Wiesner use the
four-particle encoding with frequent projection in a quantum-Zeno error
prevention scheme
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9603031)). The projection
schedule and slow independent-noise assumption are protocol claims. They do
not turn the static block into an active unknown-position corrector.

## Viewer boundary

The square arranges the four qubits so the chosen logical basis forms its
edges. The two stabilizer spokes touch every node. This is a verified
incidence scene: it says exactly which operator touches which qubit. It does
not claim a lattice Hamiltonian, nearest-neighbor extraction, a Surface-code
face, or a color-code cell. The tour states this before using the geometry.

documents.title: Stabilizer, logical basis, and exact distance
documents.markdown:
# Stabilizer, logical basis, and exact distance

## One theorem

The common `+1` eigenspace of `XXXX` and `ZZZZ` is a binary CSS
`[[4,2,2]]` stabilizer code. The following representatives form a symplectic
logical basis:

| logical | Pauli | support |
|---|---|---|
| `Xbar_1` | `XX__` | `{0,1}` |
| `Zbar_1` | `_Z_Z` | `{1,3}` |
| `Xbar_2` | `X_X_` | `{0,2}` |
| `Zbar_2` | `__ZZ` | `{2,3}` |

This choice is optimized for the square incidence drawing: the four supports
are its four edges. It is symplectically equivalent to the representatives
used by Meier, Eastin, and Knill
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4221)).

## CSS rank calculation

In binary CSS form,

`H_X = [1 1 1 1]`, and `H_Z = [1 1 1 1]`.

Their product is `H_X H_Z^T = 4 mod 2 = 0`, so the checks commute. Each
matrix has rank one and the X and Z symplectic rows are independent. Hence

`k = n - rank(S) = 4 - 2 = 2`.

The constructor creates exactly these rows from the Pauli strings and the
verifier recomputes the rank.

## Logical commutation

For CSS Pauli operators, an X-type support and a Z-type support anticommute
exactly when their intersection has odd size. The chosen supports obey

| | `Zbar_1 {1,3}` | `Zbar_2 {2,3}` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `Xbar_1 {0,1}` | one | zero |
| `Xbar_2 {0,2}` | zero | one |

Thus each numbered pair anticommutes and the cross-pairs commute. Every row
has even intersection with the opposite-type global stabilizer, so it lies in
the normalizer. No row is in the two-dimensional stabilizer row space.

## Codewords

Choose simultaneous `Zbar_1,Zbar_2` eigenstates:

`|00bar>=(|0000>+|1111>)/sqrt(2)`,

`|01bar>=(|1010>+|0101>)/sqrt(2)`,

`|10bar>=(|1100>+|0011>)/sqrt(2)`,

`|11bar>=(|0110>+|1001>)/sqrt(2)`.

Every computational string has even Hamming weight, hence eigenvalue `+1`
under `ZZZZ`. `XXXX` complements all four bits and exchanges the two terms
inside each superposition, hence also has eigenvalue `+1`. The two Z logicals
give the signs encoded in the labels, while the two X logicals permute the
four states in the expected bit directions. `reproduce.py` checks these
statements as matrices, so normalization and phase conventions are not left
to inspection.

## Exact distance

Every weight-one Pauli anticommutes with at least one stabilizer:

- `X_i` anticommutes with `ZZZZ`;
- `Z_i` anticommutes with `XXXX`;
- `Y_i` anticommutes with both.

Therefore no weight-one Pauli is a nontrivial normalizer element and `d>=2`.
But `XX__=Xbar_1` is a weight-two normalizer element outside the stabilizer,
so `d<=2`. These two constructive bounds give `d=2`. The generic exact CSS
enumerator independently returns the same value.

Rains proves the stronger classification statement: the optimal distance-two
code of length four is unique up to local equivalence
([primary source](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9704043)). That theorem
supports the identity history; the Atlas constructor still fixes one exact
binary CSS representative so downstream computation is unambiguous.
